ety.text: From Middle English der, deer (“animal, deer”), from Old English dēor (“animal”), from Proto-West Germanic *deuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewsóm (“living thing”), from *dʰéws (“breath”), full-grade derivative of *dʰwes-. Cognate with Scots deer (“deer”), North Frisian dier (“animal, beast”), West Frisian dier (“animal, beast”), Dutch dier (“animal, beast”), German Low German Deer, Deert (“animal”), German Tier (“animal, beast”), Swedish djur (“animal, beast”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk dyr (“animal, beast”), Icelandic dýr (“animal, beast”).

senses.d: A ruminant mammal with hooves and often antlers, of the family Cervidae, or one of several similar animals from related families of the order Artiodactyla, such as the musk deer or mouse deer.
ex: Deer sperm was in used among the Romans as an aphrodisiac.

senses.d: Such a mammal that is in the family Cervidae.
One of the smaller animals of the family Cervidae, distinguished from a moose or elk.
ex: I wrecked my car after a deer ran across the road.
Sure, most of us hunt deer around here, but not many of us have ever hunted moose.

senses.d: The meat of such an animal, obtained through the process of hunting or from specialized deer farms; venison.
ex: I'd never had deer before I ate dinner with the Johanssens. In time I learned to like it; its gaminess is an acquired taste.

senses.d: Any animal, especially a quadrupedal mammal as opposed to a bird, fish, etc.
ex: But mice and rats and such small deer, have been Tom's food for seven long year.

senses.d: Extending far down from the top, or surface, to the bottom, literally or figuratively.
ex: The lake is extremely deep.
We hiked into a deep valley between tall mountains.

senses.d: Positioned far from the surface or other reference point, especially down through something or into something.
ex: Diving down to deep wrecks can be dangerous.
I can't get the bullet out – it's too deep.

senses.d: Positioned far from the boundaries of or main approaches to (the specified place); interior.
ex: Impressive though Egyptian culture was, it was in deep Africa that Jung came closer to understanding himself as a man.
Films shot on location in deep Africa were still a rare exсерtion in 1960.

senses.d: Far in extent in another (non-downwards, but generally also non-upwards) direction, especially front-to-back.
ex: The shelves are 30 centimetres deep. — They are deep shelves.
That cyclist's deep chest allows him to draw more air.

senses.d: Extending to a level or length equivalent to the stated thing.
ex: The water was waist-deep.
There is an arm-deep hole in the wall.

senses.d: In a (specified) number of rows or layers.
ex: a crowd four deep along the funeral procession, with people two deep on the sidewalks
The fleet of ships was fifty sail deep.

senses.d: Voluminous.
ex: to take a deep breath / sigh / drink

senses.d: Far from the center of the playing area, near to the boundary of the playing area, either in absolute terms or relative to a point of reference.
ex: He is fielding at deep mid wicket.
She hit a ball into deep center field.

senses.d: Penetrating a long way, especially a long way forward.
ex: a deep volley
a deep run into the opposition half

senses.d: Positioned back, or downfield, towards one's own goal, or towards or behind one's baseline or similar reference point.
ex: Our defensive live is too deep. We need to move further up the field.
She returns serve from a very deep position.

senses.d: Far, especially far down through something or into something, physically or figuratively.
ex: The ogre lived in a cave deep underground.
We ventured deep into the forest.

senses.d: In a profound, not superficial, manner.
ex: I thought long and deep.

senses.d: In large volume.

senses.d: Back towards one's own goal, baseline, or similar.
ex: He's normally a midfield player, but today he's playing deep.

senses.d: The deep part of a lake, sea or ocean.
ex: creatures of the deep

senses.d: The sea, the ocean.
A deep hole or pit, a water well; an abyss.
ex: Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterfalls: All thy waves and thy billows are gone over me.

senses.d: A deep or innermost part of something in general.
A silent time; quiet isolation.

senses.d: A deep shade of colour.

ety.text: From Middle English dede, from Old English dēd, dǣd (“deed, act”), from Proto-West Germanic *dādi, from Proto-Germanic *dēdiz (“deed”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tis (“deed, action”). Analyzable through Proto-Germanic as do + -th. Doublet of thesis. The real estate sense derives from the fact that property deeds are traditionally used to demonstrate proof of ownership of a legal title in common law jurisdictions, such as England & Wales and most of the United States.

senses.d: An action or act; something that is done.
ex: One small deed can have one strong effect or more.
And Joseph said to them, What deed is this which ye have done?

senses.d: A brave or noteworthy action; a feat or exploit.

senses.d: Action or fact, as opposed to rhetoric or deliberation.

senses.d: A legal instrument that is executed under seal or before a witness; sometimes required for certain legal activities, such as the transfer of certain kinds of property.
